items.summary:
Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20 years of HN to 6,454 videos that keep being recommended. *Significantly* better viewing experience, ~2 hours with Opus 5.5:
https://t.co/JIhXN7OSh1

- Excellent recs without any logins (state is kept in local browser session)
- Thumbnail is a representative frame from middle of the video instead of the super duper A/B test hyper-optimized user uploads
- Underlying data from the comment analysis as one zip file, point your Claude at it and ask for your own version
- HackerTube Longs ✊

A bit more on the process:
I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac), Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I only talk to Claude and have it do everything, the only "manual work" I helped with in tandem was in the browser (reminiscent of MenuGen): 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box for serving and 3) I bought the domain name. Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, secure, harden, deploy and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

Many awesome projects that would have normally taken weeks/months even can now be few-shotted for breakfast. What else are we not thinking of.

items.title: Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now les
items.summary:
Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel.

- Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all.
- Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract.
- Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code.
- And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while.

The funnel is driven by a combination of factors:
1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel.
2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel.
3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal.

So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.

items.title: What is retrieval augmented generation?| Glossary | Cohesity
items.summary:
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is an NLP technique that combines retrieval-based AI, which finds relevant information from existing sources, with generative AI, which synthesizes that information into a coherent, contextually appropriate response. RAG was developed specifically to overcome the weaknesses of each approach alone: pure generative models can produce low-quality or inaccurate output on complex topics, while pure retrieval models are limited by the data they can access, and [...] Retrieval augmented generation (RAG) is a natural language processing (NLP) technique that combines the strengths of both retrieval- and generative-based artificial intelligence (AI) models. RAG AI can deliver accurate results that make the most of pre-existing knowledge but can also process and consolidate that knowledge to create unique, context-aware answers, instructions, or explanations in human-like language rather than just summarizing the retrieved data. [...] RAG was developed to overcome these relative weaknesses in existing models to combine their strengths and minimize drawbacks.

A retrieval model is used to find relevant information from existing sources in a RAG-based AI system. In contrast, the generative model takes the retrieved information, synthesizes all the data, and shapes it into a coherent and contextually appropriate response.

items.title: 385 people bookmarked a post this week whose first tip was:
items.summary:
385 people bookmarked a post this week whose first tip was:
"Turn off most of your skills, plugins, and MCPs."

It came from a 1,700-follower account.

Sounds backwards. More tools should mean more help.

Here's why fewer tools gets you better answers, and the 5 questions that decide what stays.

The reason is simple.
Every connected tool is a question the AI asks itself on every turn: do I need this one?

10 connectors means 10 small decisions before it even starts your task.
That costs time, tokens, and focus.

And agents are still bad at picking the right tool.
So the extra options mostly add wrong turns.

Here's the audit. Run it on every connector, plugin, custom GPT, and saved skill you have:

1. Did I use it in the last 14 days?
No? Turn it off. You can turn it back on in 30 seconds.

2. Can the AI already do this with plain web search or a pasted file?
If copy-paste does the job, the tool is overhead.

3. Does it touch a task I do every week?
Your top 3 weekly tasks earn a tool. Everything else waits.

4. Does it overlap with another tool?
Two note apps, two calendars, two search plugins. Keep one.

5. Would I notice if it vanished tomorrow?
If the honest answer is "probably not", it goes.

Aim for 3 to 5 tools left.

Here's the part nobody tells you:
a tool you drop is easy to bring back. The context it burns on every single turn is gone for good.

Run it once this week. Set a reminder to run it again in 30 days.

Reply with how many tools you had before and after. I want to know the average.

items.summary:
؜هي أنك لو قلت للروبوت «لا تسكب القهوة على اللابتوب»، FLEX يستخدم نموذج اللغة GPT-4o عشان يستنتج إن المقصود كمان يبعد عن باقي الأجهزة الإلكترونية والأشياء اللي تنكسر، وليس اللابتوب فقط.

؜والطريقة تمر بثلاث خطوات: تضيف الشيء اللي ذكرته، وتعمّم على الأشياء المشابهة، وتشيل الأشياء اللي ما عادت موجودة. وحسب الباحثين، كل هذا ياخذ حوالي 5 ثواني.

items.title: Study explores how AI use affects performance on math and reasoning tasks
items.summary:
The findings backed up what anecdotes and surveys have increasingly found in recent years: An overreliance on AI for answers erodes our cognitive fitness. When AI produces answers in seconds, we get used to that speed; anything that takes longer feels inefficient. And relying on AI also removes what the team called “productive struggle,” which can lead people to find their research strengths and passions. [...] For the first experiment with 354 participants, one group was tasked with solving 15 basic fraction problems without help, while another had ChatGPT open on the side to use for assistance and to even ask for the answer. The group with AI access started off more accurate than the group without it. Then, after 12 problems, researchers took away the AI tool. Almost immediately, the people in that group stopped solving questions accurately. [...] Frontier AI companies have acknowledged how offloading tasks to chatbots can reduce one’s baseline understanding and mastery of a subject. Instead of defaulting to quick answers, AI responses could default to being more instructive, like a tutor, Christian said.

“We need to work toward a future in which human abilities are, as much as possible, augmented rather than supplanted,” he said.

items.title: AI models may be capable of self-replicating without access to a datacenter \ Anthropic
items.summary: In cyber, a worm is a program that copies itself from one computer to the next without human input. Prior work has already shown that AI agents can act like one: scanning their network, executing an exploit, and copying model weights to a target machine across a GPU cluster. Such an “AI worm” could carry its model weights with it as it reproduces (or re-download them from a public hub), and then run inference directly on compromised hardware. Effectively, the weights would become part of the [...] A model that’s too large to fit on one device can be split into pieces, or shards, that run on separate machines that communicate with each other to collectively run the model. Machines that could run a significant model shard for a <30B model include smart fridges, smart ovens, automatic vacuum cleaners, and lawnmowers. A growing number of home and business devices, such as security cameras and video-conferencing units now ship with small built-in AI chips, designed to run AI models on the [...] Hard-coded botnets like the Kimwolf botnet each target a specific type of device – in Kimwolf’s case, Android TVs and mobile devices. items.title: Vulnerability Discovery and Exploitation Trends in the AI Era | Google Cloud Blog
items.summary:
### Introduction

Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) examines vulnerability disclosure and exploitation statistics to evaluate the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on the vulnerability threat landscape. We found that AI is measurably changing not just the pace of vulnerability discovery and exploitation, but also the types and typical risk profiles of vulnerabilities that are being discovered.

Key findings: [...] Centralized AI Gateways and Lateral Cloud Movement: Enterprise AI gateways represent a catastrophic dual-threat vector. At the application layer, compromised gateways expose third-party application programming interface (API) keys and private prompt streams containing personally identifiable information (PII) or proprietary source code. At the infrastructure layer, they act as initial footholds for adversaries to harvest database credentials and pivot laterally into internal cloud environments. [...] As enterprise adoption of generative AI accelerates, security research and adversary interest have also focused on vulnerabilities in the underlying AI operational stack.
